newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese officials admit phone tapping.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese officials admit phone tapping.

text.p: Lebanese officials have admitted for the first time that telephones, including cellular phones, were being tapped in the country.
"Even my conversations are being tapped," Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri told parliament jokingly during a late-night debate on Wednesday.
Deputies and officials alike challenged a statement by Interior Minister Michel al-Murr that cellular telephones were not tapped and that political authorities were unaware of what was going on.

"This issue is only limited to the security and judicial authorities and tapped lines do not exceed 60 or 70 lines," Murr said in response to a parliamentary question alleging that security or military agencies were tapping cellular telephones.
"Today we are in a critical phase in terms of security, much more critical than the phases of (the 1975-90 civil) war, and the need for tapping to protect national security has doubled," he added.
Wire tapping is only permitted in Lebanon on authorisation of a judge.
Speaker Nabih Berri responded to Murr's statement by saying: "I am certain that cellular phones are being tapped and this is very dangerous." More than one security service was involved, he said.
Berri ordered the formation of a special parliamentary committee to probe the issue.
Nassib Lahoud, an opposition deputy, said senior officials received daily reports from security forces on intercepted conversations.
"More than five people here (in parliament) today receive those reports. Therefore politicians cannot say they are not involved in phone tapping," he said.

Selim al-Hoss, a former prime minister who first raised the phone tapping issue in parliament last month, told the house he was satisfied that for the first time "the state has recognised the existence of phone tapping".
He said senior officials were involved and compared the issue to the Watergate phone-tapping scandal in the United States which toppled president Richard Nixon.
